hfaqs.a: No. Start with spoken Urdu in Roman letters, and let the script come second. Learners who speak first stay motivated far longer than learners who drill letters for a month before saying a word.
hfaqs.q: Must I learn the Urdu script before speaking?

hfaqs.a: السلام علیکم for respect, ہاں and نہیں, شکریہ, معاف کیجیے, ٹھیک ہے, and میں — I. With those seven you can open any interaction politely while your vocabulary grows underneath.
hfaqs.q: Which words should I learn in week one?

hfaqs.a: The retroflexes and Persian-Arabic sounds — ع غ ق خ — plus reading right-to-left. Ten minutes of daily listening retunes your ears within weeks; the pronunciation page walks you through each one.
hfaqs.q: What is the hardest part of Urdu?

Each phrase speaks in a native Urdu voice. Slow it to 0.2× and repeat until it sticks.
Every topic ends in practice: quiz yourself, then review the words until they stay.

title: Urdu

topics.desc: السلام علیکم and beyond — greet with warmth from your first word. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: السلام علیکم with hand on heart — respectful everywhere. Casual ہیلو works with friends; السلام علیکم never fails.
faqs.q: How do I say hello respectfully?

faqs.a: آپ کیسے ہیں؟ (formal) or تم کیسے ہو؟ (informal) — and answer میں ٹھیک ہوں، شکریہ (I'm fine, thanks). Health-questions open hearts.
faqs.q: How do I ask how someone is?

faqs.a: صبح بخیر (good morning), شب بخیر (good night), آداب (respectful greeting). Time-greetings show care; use them generously.

topics.lede: السلام علیکم and beyond — greet with warmth from your first word.
topics.note: A note on السلام علیکم. السلام علیکم (assalam-o-alaikum — peace be upon you) carries a hand on the heart and genuine warmth — the universal key. Answer وعلیکم السلام (and upon you be peace). Respect first, everything else follows.
paras: Greetings open every door: السلام علیکم (respectful hello), آداب (courteous hello), ہیلو (casual hi). Hand on heart, say السلام علیکم, and doors open — bazaars, offices, homes. One phrase, infinite welcome.

Health-questions show you care: آپ کیسے ہیں؟ (how are you, formal), میں ٹھیک ہوں (I'm fine), اور آپ؟ (and you?). Urdu small talk runs on genuine enquiry — ask properly, listen properly, belong quickly.
Time splits the day: صبح بخیر (good morning), شب بخیر (good night). Morning greetings before noon, شب بخیر only at parting — timing your بخیر shows cultural fluency.

Partings promise return: خدا حافظ (goodbye), پھر ملیں گے (we'll meet again), اپنا خیال رکھیے (take care). Rarely goodbye without a next meeting — پھر ملیں گے assumes friendship continues. Say it warmly; mean it always.
topics.title: Saying hello the Urdu way

topics.desc: ا ب پ to ی ے — the Perso-Arabic alphabet, right-to-left, made friendly. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: 39 letters — Arabic's set plus پ چ ٹ ڈ ڑ ژ ں ے and more. Same right-to-left flow, extra Indo-Persian sounds.
Almost all letters join within words — initial, middle, final shapes. Practice joining early; reading flows from writing.
The vowel-bearers ا آ ع plus ب پ ت ٹ — then ج چ ح خ. Sounds before shapes; reading follows speaking.

topics.lede: ا ب پ to ی ے — the Perso-Arabic alphabet, right-to-left, made friendly.

links.desc: Letters from zero, step by step.
links.label: Urdu basics

topics.note: A note on right-to-left. Urdu flows right-to-left — start at the right edge and glide leftwards. ا ب پ ت reads a-ba-pa-ta. Eyes adjust within days; soon left-to-right scripts feel backwards.
paras: Vowels anchor everything: ا آ (a/aa), ع (i/e carrier), ے (e), و (o/u carrier). Long-short pairs matter — دل (heart) vs دیل differs by dots and shape. Chant letters in order daily; the mouth memorises what the ear repeats.

Consonants march in families: ب پ ت ٹ (lips-teeth), ج چ ح خ (throat-palate), د ڈ ذ ر ڑ (tongue-tip), س ش ص ز (hissers). Family by family, feel where each sound lives — Urdu pronunciation is geography you can touch.
Special letters crown the set: ع غ ق (deep throat), خ (guttural kh), ژ (Persian zh), ں (nasal noon). خبر (news) shows خ in action; عشق (love) shows ع. Special letters, everyday words.
Joining grids it all: ب + ا = با, م + ی + ں = میں — letters melt into words. Write joining drills daily; reading unlocks when hands know the shapes. Script becomes a friend for life.
topics.title: Urdu alphabet

topics.desc: ایک دو تین to سو — count, pay and bargain in Urdu. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: ایک دو تین چار پانچ چھ سات آٹھ نو دس — chant to ten, then گیارہ بارہ تیرہ to twenty. Rhythm first, precision follows.
بیس (20), تیس (30), چالیس (40), پچاس (50) — then combine: اکیس (21), بتیس (32). Tens plus units, endlessly.
سو (100), ہزار (1000), لاکھ (100,000). کتنے؟ (how many?) asks; numbers answer. Markets run on these three.

topics.lede: ایک دو تین to سو — count, pay and bargain in Urdu.
topics.note: A note on کتنے؟ کتنے؟ (kitne — how much / how many?) is the most useful question — کتنے روپے؟ (how many rupees?), کتنے بجے؟ (what time is it?). One word, every transaction. Ask کتنے fearlessly; numbers come to you.
paras: One to ten sings: ایک دو تین چار پانچ چھ سات آٹھ نو دس — chant it walking, cooking, waiting. Urdu numbers love rhythm; your tongue learns faster than your brain. Ten numbers, total freedom in every shop.
Teens climb steadily: گیارہ بارہ تیرہ چودہ پندرہ سولہ سترہ اٹھارہ انیس بیس — eleven to twenty. انیس (19) and بیس (20) open the tens; climb daily and teens become trivial.
Tens multiply power: بیس تیس چالیس پچاس ساٹھ ستر اسی نوے سو — 20 to 100. Combine freely: اکیس (21), پچیس (25), ستائیس (27) — the tongue-twisters that prove fluency.
Hundreds rule markets: سو (100), دو سو (200), ہزار (1000), لاکھ (100,000). ڈیڑھ سو (150) and اڑھائی سو (250) charm shopkeepers — halves and quarters in pure Urdu. Money talks; count it in Urdu.
topics.title: Counting in Urdu

topics.desc: میں, آپ, ہاں, نہیں — hold your first real Urdu conversations. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: آپ کا نام کیا ہے؟ (what's your name?) — answer میرا نام راہل ہے (my name is Rahul). Names first, friendship follows.
faqs.q: How do I ask someone's name?

faqs.a: ہاں (yes), نہیں (no) — short, clear, universal. جی ہاں adds respect; نا is casual. Yes-no fluency first.
مجھے سمجھ نہیں آیا (I didn't understand) and آہستہ بولیے (please speak slowly). Honesty tunes every speaker to your level.

topics.lede: میں, آپ, ہاں, نہیں — hold your first real Urdu conversations.

links.desc: Dialogues with audio, step by step.
links.label: Urdu conversation lessons

topics.note: A note on مجھے. مجھے (mujhe — to-me) is Urdu's magic word — مجھے چاہیے (I want), مجھے سمجھ آیا (I understood), مجھے معلوم ہے (I know). Experiences flow TOWARD you in Urdu; master مجھے and fifty sentences unlock.
paras: People anchor talk: میں (I), آپ (you formal), وہ (he/she/they). میں اردو سیکھتا ہوں (I'm learning Urdu) — gender shows on verbs, proudly. Introduce yourself; conversations ignite.
Questions drive dialogue: کیا؟ (what?), کہاں؟ (where?), کب؟ (when?), کیوں؟ (why?), کیسے؟ (how?). آپ کہاں رہتے ہیں؟ (where do you live?) — one question word plus any verb equals conversation.
Politeness oils everything: براہ کرم (please) and معاف کیجیے (sorry/excuse me). معاف کیجیے، آہستہ بولیے (sorry, speak slowly) — apologies plus requests, the learner's armour.
Repair keeps talk alive: مجھے سمجھ نہیں آیا (I didn't understand), پھر کہیے (please say again), اس کا مطلب کیا ہے؟ (what does this mean?). Broken Urdu beats silent perfection — stumble forward daily.
topics.title: Real Urdu conversation

topics.desc: ہے, جانا, کرنا — the verbs that carry every Urdu sentence. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: میں ہوں (I am), تم ہو, وہ ہے, ہم ہیں, آپ ہیں, وہ ہیں. Being first, everything else after.
Present uses root + تا/تی/تے + ہے: میں کرتا ہوں (I do, m), میں کرتی ہوں (f). Gender shows on every present verb.
faqs.q: How does the present tense work?

faqs.a: جانا (to go), آنا (to come), کرنا (to do), کھانا (to eat), بولنا (to speak). Five verbs, half of daily speech.

topics.lede: ہے, جانا, کرنا — the verbs that carry every Urdu sentence.
topics.note: A note on ہوں/ہے/ہیں. The ہوں family (hun/hai/hain) is Urdu's heartbeat — میں ہوں (I am), وہ ہے (he/she is), آپ ہیں (you are). Every present-tense sentence pulses with ہ. Learn this family cold; the whole tense follows.
paras: Being grounds all: ہوں/ہے (am/is/are) — میں ہوں (I am), ہم ہیں (we are), آپ ہیں (you are), وہ ہیں (they are). ہے anchors identity, place, state — میں یہاں ہوں (I'm here), میں ٹھیک ہوں (I'm fine). Be first.
Going and coming move life: جانا (to go), آنا (to come) — میں جاتا ہوں (I go), میں آتا ہوں (I come). Direction verbs plus کہاں (where) navigate everywhere — میں لاہور جاتا ہوں (I'm going to Lahore).
Doing and eating fill days: کرنا (to do), کھانا (to eat), پینا (to drink) — میں کام کرتا ہوں (I work), میں کھاتا ہوں (I eat). Daily verbs, daily use; conjugate them in your sleep.
Speaking and knowing crown all: بولنا (to speak), پڑھنا (to read), لکھنا (to write) — میں اردو بولتا ہوں (I speak Urdu). Say it now, imperfectly; say it daily until the mirror agrees.
topics.title: Urdu verbs

topics.desc: پانی, گھر, کام, پیار — the hundred words Urdu daily life runs on. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Body, home, food, people: پانی (water), گھر (house), ماں (mother), دوست (friend). Concrete nouns first — point, name, own.
Adjectives agree with gender: اچھا (good-m), اچھی (f). Learn pairs together — agreement becomes music.
آج (today), کل (tomorrow), گذشتہ کل (yesterday), اب (now). Time words frame every plan — learn them this week.

topics.lede: پانی, گھر, کام, پیار — the words Urdu daily life runs on.

links.desc: Words in course order, with drills.
links.label: Urdu vocabulary

topics.note: A note on خوب. خوب (khoob — nice/great) is the universal praise — خوب ہے (it's nice), بہت خوب (very nice). Food, films, friends' work — praise everything. Generous خوب earns generous friendship.
paras: Survival nouns anchor reality: پانی (water), کھانا (food), گھر (house), راستہ (road). Point at each, say it aloud, use it today — پانی چاہیے (I want water). Concrete first, abstract later.
People words warm speech: آدمی (person), دوست (friend), ماں (mother), بچہ (child). میرا دوست (my friend) introduces proudly; ماں calls home. People before things, always.
Describing words add colour: بڑا (big), چھوٹا (small), اچھا (good), نیا (new). Adjectives dance with gender — بڑا بھائی (big brother), بڑی بہن (big sister). Pair-learn each one.
Time and feeling complete the core: آج (today), پیار (love), خوشی (joy), کام (work). آج بہت کام ہے (there's lots of work today) — then پیار اور خوشی balance it. Words for living, not just talking.
topics.title: Core Urdu vocabulary

topics.desc: بریانی to کھیر — order, eat and praise food in Urdu. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: کھانا (meal), ناشتہ (breakfast), چائے (tea). مجھے بھوک لگی ہے (I'm hungry) opens every food conversation.
faqs.q: How do I talk about meals?

faqs.a: یہ کیا ہے؟ (what is this?) and مجھے بریانی چاہیے (I want biryani). Point, ask, order — menus fear the curious.
تیز (spicy), میٹھا (sweet), نمکین (salty), کھٹا (sour). کم تیز (less spicy) saves sensitive tongues.

topics.lede: بریانی to کھیر — order, eat and praise food in Urdu.
topics.note: A note on دسترخوان. دسترخوان (dastarkhwan — the spread meal-cloth) is hospitality itself — کھانا تیار ہے (food is ready) gathers everyone. مہمان نوازی (hospitality) is sacred; guests eat first, hosts eat joy. Food is love, served hot.
paras: Meals structure the day: ناشتہ (breakfast), کھانا (lunch/dinner), چائے (tea). چائے پییں گے؟ (shall we have tea?) — life runs on doodh-patti and conversation. Accept every cup; refuse nothing twice.

Ordering is easy bravery: مجھے ایک چائے چاہیے (I want one tea), بل دیجیے (please give the bill). ایک پلیٹ بریانی دیجیے (give one plate of biryani) — order the soul of the cuisine in Urdu. Dhabas reward attempts with extra raita.

Staples fill the dastarkhwan: چاول (rice), روٹی (flatbread), دال (lentils), سبزی (vegetables). سبزی کیا ہے؟ (what's the vegetable dish?) — ask daily, eat variously. Shared eating teaches vocabulary with every bite.
Tastes tune the tongue: تیز (spicy), میٹھا (sweet) — کھیر (rice pudding) crowns feasts. کم تیز کیجیے (make it less spicy) — then بہت خوب! (very nice!). Praise the cook; second helpings follow.
topics.title: Food phrases

topics.desc: ع غ ق خ, retroflexes, poetic rhythm — speak Urdu like a native. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Deep-throat sounds: ع (voiced squeeze), غ (gargled g), ق (deep k), خ (guttural kh). Listen to newsreaders; imitate slowly. Months of music in four letters.
faqs.q: How do I pronounce ع غ ق خ?

faqs.a: ٹ ڈ ڑ — tongue curls to the roof. ٹماٹر (tomato), ڈاک (post), پڑھنا (to read). Flap them boldly; Urdu retroflexes are proud.
Long-short pairs change words. Hold long vowels fully double — Urdu ears measure length precisely.

topics.lede: ع غ ق خ, retroflexes, poetic rhythm — speak Urdu like a native.
topics.note: A note on آہستہ. آہستہ (aahistaa — slowly) is the learner's best friend — آہستہ بولیے (please speak slowly). Say it with a smile and every Urdu speaker shifts to teacher-mode. Slow speech is kind speech; ask for it freely.
paras: The deep quartet rules: عشق (love), غم (sorrow), قلم (pen), خبر (news) — throat engaged, sound resonant. Minimal pairs drill them: کال (famine) vs قال (he said) — practise قلم vs کلم daily. Master these and Urdu voices beam.
Retroflexes flap boldly: ٹماٹر (tomato), ڈاک (post), پڑھنا (to read) — tongue back, tap forward. Urdu retroflexes hit harder than Hindi's; lean into them. Bold flaps mark the insider.
Length carries meaning: short and long vowels are different letters, different words. Double the long ones fully; clip the short ones crisp. Ears measure; mouths must comply.

Rhythm ties it together: آہستہ (slowly) first, then natural speed; زور سے (loudly) for clarity, خاموش (quiet) for calm. تلفظ (pronunciation) improves with echoing — shadow newsreaders daily, record yourself weekly.
topics.title: Urdu pronunciation

topics.desc: Two genders, postpositions, verb-final order — grammar without tears. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Masculine and feminine — nouns, adjectives AND verbs agree. اچھا/اچھی (good), جاتا/جاتی (go). Pairs everywhere; learn them as sets.
کو marks direction (لاہور کو — to Lahore), نے marks doers (رام نے کیا — Ram did), سے means with/from. Postpositions follow nouns — learn each with ten examples.
Subject-Object-Verb: میں چاول کھاتا ہوں (I rice eat). Verb last, always. English order is the classic beginner error.

topics.lede: Two genders, postpositions, verb-final order — grammar without tears.
topics.note: A note on نے. نے (ne) marks the doer in past tense — رام نے کیا (Ram did), میں نے کھایا (I ate). Ergative, elegant, everywhere in stories. Tiny suffix, enormous workload.
paras: Two genders shape everything: masculine (لڑکا — boy), feminine (لڑکی — girl). Adjectives pair — اچھا/اچھی — and verbs pair too. Gender is not decoration; it is Urdu's skeleton.

Pronouns simplify persons: میں (I), تم (you-informal), آپ (you-formal), وہ (he-she/they), ہم (we). ہم vs ہم سب (we vs all-of-us) shades meaning; آپ is always plural-form, always respectful. Choose your you wisely.
Postpositions replace prepositions: -کو (to), -نے (by/doer), -سے (with/from), -میں (in). گھر کو جاؤ (go home), چمچ سے کھاؤ (eat with a spoon). Suffixes after nouns — think backwards from English.

Verbs anchor sentences last: میں چاول کھاتا ہوں (I rice eat), وہ اسکول جاتی ہے (she to-school goes). Present (کھاتا ہوں), past (کھایا), future (کھاؤں گا) — tense on verbs, time words framing. Verb-final: the one rule that never breaks.
topics.title: Urdu grammar, plainly explained

topics.desc: Zero to first conversation — your first week of Urdu, step by step. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: السلام علیکم, ہاں, نہیں, شکریہ, معاف کیجیے, ٹھیک ہے, میں — seven words that open every door. Speak them from day one.
faqs.q: What are my first seven words?

faqs.a: No — speak first in Roman letters, add Urdu script in week two. Speakers stay motivated; script-drillers quit. Talk today, read tomorrow.
Twenty focused minutes: five words, one dialogue, one song line. Daily beats marathon — streaks compound into fluency.

topics.lede: Zero to first conversation — your first week of Urdu, step by step.
topics.note: A note on آغاز. آغاز (aaghaaz — beginning) is the bravest word in Urdu — آج سے آغاز (starting from today). Every fluent speaker once said their first broken السلام علیکم. Begin badly; continue daily; arrive surely.
paras: Day one speaks: السلام علیکم (hello), ہاں (yes), نہیں (no) — say them to mirrors, pets, shopkeepers. Pronunciation need not be perfect; attempts earn smiles and corrections. Speaking starts speaking; nothing else does.
Days two to four add survival: شکریہ (thanks), معاف کیجیے (sorry), پانی (water), کتنے؟ (how much?). Four days, seven words, infinite transactions. Survival Urdu fits in a pocket and works everywhere.

Days five to seven build sentences: میں استاد ہوں (I am a teacher), مجھے چائے چاہیے (I want tea), آپ کیسے ہیں؟ (how are you?). Frames plus words equal conversation — slots fill fast when frames stand ready.

Week two opens the script: ا ب پ, then ج چ ح خ — Urdu script through familiar words. Read what you already say; letters become friends, not walls. Speak-first learners read faster — motivation decodes.
topics.title: Urdu for absolute beginners

topics.desc: ماں, ابا, دادی, دادا — family words that open homes. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: ماں (mother), ابا (father), بھائی (brother), بہن (sister). Family first — people ask about yours within minutes.
چچا (uncle), چچی (aunt), دادی (grandmother), دادا (grandfather). Extended family, extended vocabulary.
میرا خاندان بڑا ہے (my family is big) — میری ماں استانی ہے (my mother is a teacher). Describe yours; hearts open.
faqs.q: How do I describe my family?

topics.lede: ماں, ابا, دادی, دادا — family words that open homes.
topics.note: A note on دادی. دادی (daadi — grandmother) rules hearts — دادی کی کہانیاں (grandmother's stories) raised generations. Learn دادی and دادا (grandfather); elders glow when learners speak family. Respect the roots; the tree welcomes you.
paras: Parents anchor all: ماں (mother), ابا (father) — میری ماں (my mother), میرے ابا (my father). Children chant ماں first; learners should too. Home begins here.

Siblings share childhood: بھائی (brother), بہن (sister), بڑا بھائی (elder brother), بڑی بہن (elder sister). بڑا marks respect for age — birth order lives in address. Call elders rightly; love follows.

Grandparents crown memory: دادی (grandmother), دادا (grandfather) — story-keepers, sweet-givers, wisdom-wells. میری دادی پیاری کہانی سناتی ہے (my grandmother tells lovely stories) — everyone smiles. Honour them in speech.
The household gathers: خاندان (family), گھر (home), شادی (wedding), بچہ (child). میرا خاندان بڑا ہے (my family is big) — then listen; people narrate families with epic joy. Share yours; hear theirs.
topics.title: Family words

topics.desc: کتنے بجے؟ پیر to اتوار — time, days and dates in Urdu. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: کتنے بجے؟ (how much has struck?) — answer پانچ بجے (five o'clock). Time strikes in Urdu; ask it everywhere.
faqs.q: How do I ask the time?

faqs.a: پیر منگل بدھ جمعرات جمعہ ہفتہ اتوار — chant the week; planet-days roll musically.
آج (today), کل (tomorrow), گذشتہ کل (yesterday), پرسوں (day after/before). Four words frame every plan.

topics.lede: کتنے بجے؟ پیر to اتوار — time, days and dates.
topics.note: A note on بجے. بجے (baje — has struck) makes time musical — کتنے بجے؟ (how much has struck?), پانچ بجے (five has struck). Clocks strike, bells ring, Urdu asks poetically. Time doesn't pass; it chimes.
paras: Clock time strikes: کتنے بجے؟ (what time?), ایک بجا (one o'clock), پانچ بجے (five o'clock). ساڑھے پانچ (5:30), پونے چھ (5:45), سوا چھ (6:15) — halves and quarters sing. Ask time daily; numbers stick.
Day parts flow: صبح (morning), دوپہر (afternoon), شام (evening), رات (night). صبح کو (in the morning), رات کو (at night) — suffixes time the day. Parts first, precision after.
Weeks cycle planet-wise: پیر (Monday) through اتوار (Sunday). آج پیر ہے (today is Monday) — date yourself daily. Weekdays rhythm life.
Dates frame plans: آج (today), کل (tomorrow), گذشتہ کل (yesterday), تاریخ (date). کل ملیں گے؟ (shall we meet tomorrow?) — propose, confirm, arrive. Plans in Urdu keep in Urdu.
topics.title: Time and dates

topics.desc: ٹکٹ, اسٹیشن, کہاں؟ — travel by train, bus and word. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: ریلوے اسٹیشن کہاں ہے؟ (where is the railway station?) — swap in بس اڈا, ہوائی اڈا. Where-questions navigate nations.
ٹکٹ کتنے کا؟ (how much is the ticket?) and ایک ٹکٹ دیجیے (give one ticket). Tickets first, journeys after.
دائیں (right), بائیں (left), سیدھا (straight). دائیں مڑیے (turn right) — direct and be directed.

topics.lede: ٹکٹ, اسٹیشن, کہاں؟ — travel by train, bus and word.
topics.note: A note on سفر. سفر (safar — journey) is pure romance — ریل کا سفر (train journey) through plains and old cities, winter fog on windows. سفر بخیر (happy journey) blesses every traveller. Journey well; arrive storied.
paras: Stations start journeys: ریلوے اسٹیشن (railway station), بس اڈا (bus stand), ہوائی اڈا (airport). اسٹیشن کہاں ہے؟ (where is the station?) — ask anyone; people direct travellers with pride.
Tickets buy passage: ٹکٹ (ticket) — ایک ٹکٹ دیجیے (give one ticket), ٹکٹ کتنے کا؟ (how much?). گاڑی کب آئے گی؟ (when will the train come?) — گاڑی means both train and car; context steers.
Directions decode cities: دائیں (right), بائیں (left), سیدھا (straight), نزدیک (near), دور (far). سیدھا جائیے، پھر دائیں (go straight, then right) — follow, arrive, thank.
Stays shelter nights: ہوٹل (hotel), کمرہ (room), پتہ (address). کمرہ کتنے کا؟ (how much for a room?) — bargain smiling, sleep soundly. سفر ends in rest; rest remakes travellers.
topics.title: Travel phrases

topics.desc: قیمت, رعایت, رنگ — shop in Urdu from first price to final deal. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: اس کی قیمت کیا ہے؟ (what's the price of this?) — then بس کتنے؟ (just how much?) for everything else. Two questions, every shop.
faqs.q: How do I ask the price?

faqs.a: بہت مہنگا ہے (too costly) with a smile, then تھوڑا کم کیجیے (reduce a little). Bargaining is friendly theatre — play your part warmly and the price moves.
Start with five: لال (red), نیلا (blue), ہرا (green), پیلا (yellow), سفید (white). اور رنگ دکھائیے (show another colour) reveals the rest.

topics.lede: قیمت, رعایت, رنگ — shop in Urdu from first price to final deal.

topics.note: A note on تھوڑا کم کیجیے. تھوڑا کم کیجیے (thodaa kam keejiye — please reduce a little) is the magic sentence of every bazaar. Said smiling, it opens every negotiation; said with لوں گا (I'll take it) right after, it closes most. Bargaining respects the dance, never the demand.
paras: Prices open every transaction: اس کی قیمت کیا ہے؟ (what's this one's price?), کتنے روپے؟ (how many rupees?). Listen for the number, repeat it back — پچاس؟ (fifty?) — and you are already shopping in Urdu.

Bargaining follows the friendly script: بہت مہنگا ہے (too costly), رعایت دیجیے (give a discount), تھوڑا کم کیجیے (reduce a little). Start walking away slowly — اچھا، دیکھتا ہوں (okay, I'll look around) — and the real price often chases you down the street.

Sizes and colours refine the hunt: بڑا دیجیے (give the big one), چھوٹا دیجیے (give the small one), نیا دکھائیے (show a new one), اور رنگ (another colour). Point, name the change, nod — shopkeepers read gestures fluently and reward attempts instantly.

Colours close the sale: لال (red), نیلا (blue), ہرا (green), پیلا (yellow), سفید (white), کالا (black). لال خوب لگتا ہے (the red looks nice) — then لوں گا (I'll take it). Deal done, in Urdu, with a smile on both sides.
topics.title: Shopping and bargaining

topics.desc: مدد, ڈاکٹر, ہسپتال — emergency Urdu you hope to never need. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: مجھے مدد کیجیے (please help me) — loud, clear, repeated. Add ہسپتال کہاں ہے؟ (where is the hospital?) and crowds mobilise instantly.
faqs.q: What is the one emergency sentence?

faqs.a: Point and say یہاں درد ہے (it hurts here). Then مجھے اچھا نہیں لگ رہا (I feel unwell) and ڈاکٹر کو بلائیے (call a doctor). Pain plus pointing crosses every language gap.
کھو گیا (it is lost) — پیسے کھو گئے (money lost), بیگ کھو گیا (bag lost). Then پولیس اسٹیشن کہاں ہے؟ (where is the police station?).
faqs.q: How do I report something lost?

topics.lede: مدد, ڈاکٹر, ہسپتال — emergency Urdu you hope to never need.
topics.note: A note on مدد. مدد (madad — help) is Urdu's shortest lifeline — shout it and crowds come running. Bystander culture is famously kind: strangers will escort you to hospitals, translate for doctors, and refuse thanks. Ask loudly; receive gratefully.
paras: The core three save lives: مدد (help), خطرہ (danger), فوری مدد (urgent help). مجھے مدد کیجیے (please help me) — say it to anyone, anywhere. Crowds respond to distress calls faster than any app; your job is only to ask.

Medical words route the rescue: ڈاکٹر (doctor), ہسپتال (hospital), دوا (medicine), میڈیکل اسٹور (pharmacy). ہسپتال کہاں ہے؟ (where is the hospital?) plus a taxi wave — in cities, help arrives in minutes.

Symptoms speak simply: یہاں درد ہے (it hurts here, point!), مجھے اچھا نہیں لگ رہا (I feel unwell), سر درد (headache), بخار (fever). Pain words plus pointing hands diagnose across every language barrier on earth.

Danger and loss close the kit: آگ (fire), چور (thief), پولیس (police), کھو گیا (it's lost), سفارتخانہ (embassy). Memorise these cold — emergencies never wait for phrasebooks, and ten minutes of drilling buys total peace of mind.
topics.title: Emergency Urdu

topics.desc: آپ or تم؟ آئیے or آ؟ Respect levels, decoded with examples. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: آپ for every adult you don't know well — shopkeepers, officials, elders, strangers. تم waits for close friends, children and family. Wrong-side errors embarrass; learners are forgiven, but respect first is always safest.
Use the -یے form: آ becomes آئیے, جا becomes جائیے, کہہ becomes کہیے. One ending, instant politeness — the highest-value sound in Urdu.
faqs.q: How do I make a command polite?

faqs.a: جناب (sir) and محترمہ (madam) for strangers. جناب، وقت کیا ہے؟ (sir, what time is it?). Better than pointing and shouting in any language.

topics.lede: آپ or تم؟ آئیے or آ؟ Respect levels, decoded.
topics.note: A note on -یے. The -یے ending (ye) is Urdu's respect rocket — آئیے (do come), دیکھیے (please see), کہیے (please tell). One sound that upgrades every request instantly. Stem-alone orders bark; -یے invites.
paras: Urdu has two yous: آپ (formal and plural — strangers, elders, officials) and تم (familiar — friends, children, family). English erased this distinction centuries ago; Urdu keeps it razor-sharp. Every conversation opens with an invisible choice — make it consciously, and make it respectful.

Verbs mirror the split: آئیے (please come) versus آؤ (come!), کہیے (please say) versus کہو (say!), جائیے (please go) versus جاؤ (go!). The -یے ending is pure respect — same verb, different universe. Stems bark; -یے invites.

Giving and forgiving show the range: دیجیے (please give) versus دو (give, familiar), معاف کیجیے (please forgive) versus معاف کرو (forgive, familiar). Beggars and kings both hear دیجیے — politeness in Urdu costs nothing and buys everything.

Strangers get titles: جناب (sir), صاحب (mister), محترمہ (madam). جناب، مدد کیجیے (sir, please help) opens any door; barking orders at strangers closes them. Urdu warmth is earned with two syllables of respect.
topics.title: Formal and informal Urdu

topics.desc: Verb-first sentences, میں چاہیے, نہیں vs نہ — fix the classic errors. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: English order with Urdu words: میں جا instead of میں جاتا ہوں, verb first, question words misplaced. Cure: every sentence ends with the verb — practise SOV until English order feels foreign.
faqs.q: What is the most common mistake?

faqs.a: Wanting flows toward people: مجھے چاہیے (to-me it-is-wanted), never میں چاہیے. One of Urdu's deepest patterns — experiences come TO you — and beginners fight it for weeks.
نہیں denies verbs — پیسے نہیں ہیں (there's no money); نہ forbids — شور نہ کرو (don't make noise). Two no's, two jobs, zero overlap.

topics.lede: Verb-first sentences, میں چاہیے, نہیں vs نہ — fix them all.
topics.note: A note on غلطی. غلطی (ghalati — mistake) is the kindest word in this lesson — میری غلطی (my mistake) disarms every situation. Urdu speakers adore learners who err boldly and laugh warmly; the only true غلطی is silence.
paras: Mistake one: English word order. میں جا (I go — bare stem, wrong) instead of میں جاتا ہوں (I go — conjugated, right); verbs wandering mid-sentence instead of anchoring the end. Urdu is verb-final, always — SOV is not a suggestion, it is the law.

Mistake two: میں چاہیے (I want — wrong) instead of مجھے چاہیے (to-me wanted — right). Urdu wanting flows toward the wanter; English wanting fires from the wanter. Flip the arrow and dozens of sentences — مجھے سمجھ آیا, مجھے معلوم ہے — unlock at once.

Mistake three: one-size no. نہیں denies verbs — پیسے نہیں ہیں (there's no money); نہ forbids and refuses — چائے نہ (no tea for me). Beginners spray نہ everywhere; natives smile and correct. Learn both no's, use each precisely.

Mistake four: rushing sounds — flat long vowels, weak ع غ ق, wrong gender endings. آہستہ (slowly), صحیح (correctly), پھر (again): the holy trinity of repair. کوشش (effort) plus مشق (practice) plus صبر (patience) — and مبارک ہو, mistakes become fluency.

topics.desc: Stop translating in your head — shadowing, thinking aloud and brave first speeches. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Shadow natives: play an Urdu sentence, repeat it aloud half a second behind, matching rhythm and melody. Ten minutes daily rewires your mouth faster than any textbook.
faqs.q: What is the fastest speaking drill?

faqs.a: Yes — narrate your day in Urdu: میں چائے پیتا ہوں (I'm drinking tea), میں اسکول جاتا ہوں. Thinking aloud turns dead time into speaking practice.
faqs.q: Should I talk to myself in Urdu?

faqs.a: Perfectionism. Urdu speakers reward every attempt and correct with love — بولیے، غلطی کوئی بات نہیں (speak, mistakes are fine). Fluency is corrected mistakes, stacked daily.

topics.note: A note on بولیے. بولیے (boliye — let's speak, please speak) is permission and invitation in one word — آئیے، اردو میں بولیے (come, let's speak in Urdu). Say it to every patient listener; doors, hearts and vocabularies open together.
paras: Speaking starts with shadowing: play an Urdu line, echo it half a beat behind, copying music more than words. گفتگو (conversation) is rhythm before grammar — shadow ten minutes daily and your mouth learns Urdu's dance while your brain watches.

Questions and answers volley practice: سوال (question) out, جواب (answer) back. Ask yourself everything — یہ کیا ہے؟ کہاں؟ کیوں؟ — and answer aloud. Self-volleys feel silly for a day, then feel like fluency arriving.

Opinions and stories stretch speeches: رائے (opinion), سچ (truth), کہانی (story). میری رائے (in my opinion) forces full sentences; کہانی سنائیے (tell a story) forces sequences. Opinions build sentences; stories build speakers.

Courage closes the circuit: ہمت (courage) speaks first and perfects later. گیت (songs) loosen tongues, ہنسی (laughter) dissolves fear, خاموشی (pauses) are allowed. Speak badly today — تقریر (speech) improves only in motion.
topics.title: Speaking practice

topics.desc: Fast speech, films and radio — train your ears until Urdu sounds slow. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Spoken Urdu contracts: جاتا ہوں melts toward جاتوں, کرتا ہوں toward کرتوں. Learn the full forms first, then meet the street forms — this page bridges both.
faqs.q: Why is spoken Urdu so fast?

faqs.a: Children's films and songs first — clear speech, simple stories, endless repetition. Then ریڈیو dramas, then full فلم (cinema). Difficulty ladders beat difficulty cliffs.
faqs.q: What should I listen to first?

faqs.a: Catch the question words — کیا، کہاں، کون، کب — and the verb at the end. Questions plus verbs carry eighty percent of meaning; the rest is decoration.
faqs.q: How do I catch meaning in fast speech?

topics.note: A note on سمجھ آیا؟ سمجھ آیا؟ (samajh aayaa — do you understand?) is the kindest question in Urdu — teachers, friends and drivers ask it constantly. Answer سمجھ آیا (understood) or تھوڑا تھوڑا (little by little); honesty tunes every speaker to your level.
paras: Listening begins with attention: توجہ (attention) — توجہ سے سنیے (listen carefully). Urdu sentences save the verb for last, so ears must hold the whole sentence before meaning lands. Patience is a listening skill; practise holding, not guessing.

Street Urdu contracts beautifully: جاتوں، کرتوں، بولتوں — the melted present. Textbooks teach the full forms; ears must learn the melted ones. Listen for the verb-ghost at sentence end — the meaning hides there.

Media ladders the difficulty: گیت (songs) first — slow, repetitive, emotional; خبریں (news) next — clear, formal, standard; ریڈیو (radio) drama third — fast, natural, fun; فلم (films) last — slang, speed, glory. Climb rung by rung; never leap.

Active listening closes the loop: پھر سنیے (listen again), آواز (sound) by آواز. Replay each line three times — once for music, once for words, once for meaning. Three passes per line, ten lines per day: ears transform within a month.

topics.desc: Words to sentences to stories — reading Urdu from first signs to full pages. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Signboards: دکان (shop), اسٹیشن (station), ہوٹل (restaurant) — big letters, daily repetition, instant rewards. Streets teach faster than textbooks.
Children's books — short جملہ (sentences), pictures for context, full joinings. Then comics, then اخبار headlines, then articles.
faqs.q: When am I ready for books?

faqs.a: Keep a لغت (dictionary) app open and mine unknown words — five per page, no more. Reading with a dictionary beats studying word lists: context glues memory.
faqs.q: How do I handle unknown words?

topics.lede: Words to sentences to stories — reading from first signs to full pages.
topics.note: A note on اخبار. Urdu newspapers — جنگ، ایکسپریس — use formal written Urdu, nobler than street speech. Headlines first: big type, short lines, daily habit. One headline a day keeps illiteracy away.
paras: Reading starts with words: لفظ (word) by لفظ — پڑھیے (please read) signs, labels, names. Urdu spelling rewards the patient: see دکان, say dukaan, know shop. Joining practice makes readers richly.

Sentences assemble next: جملہ (sentence) — subject, object, verb-last. Read SOV sentences end-first for meaning: find the verb, then ask who-did-what. Backwards parsing feels odd for a week, then automatic forever.

Paragraphs and articles follow: پیراگراف (paragraph), مضمون (article), نظم (poem). Children's stories first — short, illustrated, kind — then رسالے (magazines), then ادب (literature) itself. Urdu's written heritage spans three centuries; start at the shallow end.

Dictionaries deepen everything: لغت (dictionary) — five new words per page, written down, reviewed nightly. Reading without recording entertains; reading with recording teaches. Mine every page; keep every gem.
topics.title: Reading Urdu

topics.desc: Letters to lists to letters — writing Urdu from first strokes to full pages. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Flowing strokes first: Urdu letters join right-to-left — ا، ب، م. Trace big, shrink slowly; لکھائی (handwriting) beautifies with mileage.
faqs.q: How do I start writing Urdu?

faqs.a: فہرست (lists): shopping lists, word lists, daily plans. Lists forgive grammar, demand spelling, and get used — the perfect beginner writing.
خط (letters) to friends, نوٹ (notes) to self, گھر کا کام (homework) for courses. Real writing to real readers beats copied exercises every time.

topics.lede: Letters to lists to letters — writing from first strokes to full pages.
topics.note: A note on دستخط. Your دستخط (signature) in Urdu script is a milestone — practise it until it flows in one confident motion. Signing Urdu-style on forms, cards and letters declares belonging more than any certificate.
paras: Writing starts with flow: Urdu letters join and glide — لکھیے (please write) curves and dots before full words. Trace ا ب پ م ن big and slow; the hand learns shapes the eye already knows.
Tools matter little, mileage matters all: قلم (pen), pencil, finger on steamed mirrors — children trace in notebooks, slates and air. Write everywhere; medium is vanity, motion is learning.

Lists graduate the hand: فہرست (list) — نوٹ (notes), پتہ (addresses), تاریخ (dates). Copy your own نام (name) fifty times, then friends' names, then street names. Familiar words, fresh script: the fastest fluent hand.
Real writing arrives: خط (letters), درخواست (applications), امتحان (exams), گھر کا کام (homework). Write a postcard to yourself in Urdu — short, joyful, posted. First posted Urdu is never forgotten.
topics.title: Writing Urdu

topics.desc: Who does what, verb last — Urdu sentences decoded with living examples. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Subject-Object-Verb: میں کتاب پڑھتا ہوں (I book read). Endings mark roles, so order flexes for emphasis — but verb-last is home.
Tense lives on the verb, with gender: پڑھتا/پڑھتی (read-present), پڑھا (read-past), پڑھوں گا (will read). Time words — گذشتہ کل، آج، کل — frame it; the verb carries it.
Rise at the end: یہ تیری کتاب ہے؟ (is this your book?). Question words — کیا، کہاں، کون — sit where the answer would.

topics.lede: Who does what, verb last — sentences decoded with living examples.
topics.note: A note on بارش ہوتی ہے. Urdu weather does things: بارش ہوتی ہے (rain happens), دھوپ نکلی ہے (sun is out), ہوا چلتی ہے (wind blows). No empty it — Urdu skies act. Weather sentences teach SOV with zero confusion: subject, then verb, done.
paras: Simple sentences stack three blocks: میں اسکول جاتا ہوں (I — to-school — go), وہ گیت گاتی ہے (she — song — sings), ہم اردو سیکھتے ہیں (we — Urdu — study). Subject, object, verb — build a hundred of these and Urdu skeleton is yours.

Animals make perfect practice: لڑکا ہنستا ہے (the boy laughs), کتا بھونکتا ہے (the dog barks), بلی سوتی ہے (the cat sleeps). Short subjects, vivid verbs, zero ambiguity — describe every creature you meet and SOV becomes reflex.

Time flexes the frame: میں کل آؤں گا (I'll come tomorrow), گذشتہ کل بارش ہوئی (it rained yesterday). Time words float — front for emphasis, middle for flow — while the verb holds the end. Tense plus time word: past, present, future, mastered.

Identity and questions close the set: یہ میرا گھر ہے (this is my house), یہ تیری کتاب ہے؟ (is this your book?), سب ٹھیک ہے (all is well). Equate with یہ/وہ, question with rising tone, reassure with سب ٹھیک ہے — sentences for every situation.
topics.title: Urdu sentence structure

topics.desc: Rahul becomes راہل — spell, write and own your name in Urdu script. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Sound it out in Urdu letters: Rahul → راہل, Priya → پریا, John → جان. Urdu spells by ear — say your name slowly, catch each sound, write each letter.
faqs.q: How do I write my name in Urdu?

faqs.a: Special letters — خ (kha), غ (gha), ق (qa), ژ (zha) — handle rich sounds. فون (phone), خبر (news) — deep letters for deep sounds, fully Urdu now.
پہلا حرف (first letter) starts it, آخری حرف (last letter) ends it. Introduce with میرا نام (my name is), then write it — introductions stick twice as well written.
faqs.q: How do I introduce my name?

topics.lede: Rahul becomes راہل — spell, write and own your name in Urdu.
topics.note: A note on راہل. Foreign names glide in Urdu script — Rahul appears as راہل, sometimes راہول with a longer vowel. All are read Rahul; none is wrong. Urdu welcomes foreign names with flexible spelling — pick the shape you love and own it.
paras: Names transliterate by ear: break yours into sounds, match each to Urdu letters — روی (Ravi), لکشمی (Lakshmi), کرن (Kiran) show the pattern. Say it slow, write it true — سپیلنگ (spelling) by sound, not by English letters.
Rich sounds get deep letters: خ for khabar-sounds (خبر), ف for phone (فون), ژ for television (ٹیلی ویژن). These deep letters are Urdu's pride — use them proudly for every rich sound.

Introductions pair speech and script: تعارف (introduction) — میرا نام (my name is), spoken, then written. نام والے بورڈ (name boards) on doors and desks teach daily — read every board, collect every name.

Nicknames warm everything: پیار کا نام (nickname) — بچو (dear child), سونا (golden one), گڑیا (little doll). Urdu shortens with love: Ravi becomes روی, Simran becomes سمی. Earn an Urdu nickname and you have arrived.

topics.desc: زبردست, یار, ایک نمبر — street Urdu that films, friends and fun run on. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: زبردست (awesome) and ایک نمبر (number one) — positive, universal, safe. Sprinkle them on food, films and friends; instant insider status.
یار (buddy) and بھائی (bro) — for friends only, never elders or strangers. Friendship slang misused offends; rightly used, it bonds instantly.
Hanging out, passing time joyfully — کیا چل رہا ہے؟ — کچھ نہیں، ٹائم پاس (what's up? — nothing, timepass). The most casual answer in existence: relaxed joy, declared proudly.

topics.lede: زبردست, یار, ایک نمبر — street Urdu that fun runs on.
topics.note: A note on چھا گئے. چھا گئے (chhaa gaye — you've overshadowed everyone, you rock!) is the ultimate praise — shouted at brilliant performances, clever jokes, winning goals. Praise loudly; belong instantly.
paras: Praise slang opens doors: زبردست (awesome), ایک نمبر (number one), چھا گئے (you rock), فرسٹ کلاس (first class), کمال (wonderful). Food, films, friends' outfits — praise everything loudly. Urdu speakers praise generously; learners should too.

Friendship words bond crews: یار (buddy), بھائی (bro), دوست (friend) — friends-only, always warm. یار، آؤ نا (come on buddy) starts a thousand conversations daily. Never aim them upward at elders; sideways at friends, fire freely.

Reaction words colour stories: ہائے اللہ (oh my God!), واہ جی واہ (wow!), گپیں نہ مارو (stop making things up!). Urdu storytelling runs on reactions — gasp, laugh, disbelieve theatrically. Flat faces kill stories; big reactions feed them.

Playful edges season everything: چل نکل (get lost — playful among friends, rude otherwise), چھی (mild disgust), ٹائم پاس (chilling). Learn the edges, respect the edges: slang's power is knowing exactly where fun ends.
topics.title: Urdu slang

topics.desc: Toys, moons, stars and good-child gold — Urdu for little learners, big joy. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Songs and کہانی (stories) — گیت with actions, tales with voices. Children absorb Urdu through music and play long before grammar.
faqs.q: How do kids learn Urdu best?

faqs.a: اچھا بچہ (good child) — praise every attempt loudly. Parenting runs on encouragement; learners of all ages bloom under it.
faqs.q: How do I praise a child?

faqs.a: کھیل (games): name objects — گیند! کھلونا! — count steps, sing counts. Play first, words hitchhike.

topics.lede: Toys, moons, stars and gold stars — Urdu for little learners, big joy.
topics.note: A note on بچو. بچو (bachcho — baby/darling) melts every heart — میرا بچو (my darling) for children, pets and beloveds. Terms of endearment are Urdu's mother tongue; every child swims in them.
paras: Little learners start with love: بچے (children), بچو (baby), سونا (golden one), اچھا بچہ (good child). Childhood floats on affection-words — call every child بچو and watch faces light like دیوالی.
Play teaches fastest: کھیل (play), کھلونا (toy), گیند (ball) — کھیلیں (let's play)! Count throws, name colours, chase and giggle. Play first; Urdu hitchhikes on joy.
School words structure days: اسکول (school), استاد (teacher), سبق (lesson), گھر کا کام (homework). السلام علیکم سر (hello sir) opens every school day — respect and learning, hand in hand.

Sky words spark wonder: سورج (sun), چاند (moon), تارا (star) — چاند دیکھو (look at the moon)! Night-sky Urdu, whispered on terraces, becomes lifelong memory. Teach the sky; the child keeps the language.
topics.title: Urdu for kids

topics.desc: Meetings, customers, contracts — professional Urdu for offices and business. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: السلام علیکم، میں (hello, I'm) — then آپ سے مل کر خوشی ہوئی (pleased to meet you). Business Urdu opens formal and warms slowly.
faqs.q: How do I introduce myself at work?

faqs.a: میٹنگ کب ہے؟ (when is the meeting?) and میٹنگ کہاں ہے؟ (where?). Meetings run offices — never miss one for language reasons.
faqs.q: How do I ask about meetings?

faqs.a: ای میل بھیجوں گا (I'll send an email) and فون پر بات کریں گے (let's talk on the phone). Digital Urdu borrows freely — clarity beats purity in business.

topics.lede: Meetings, customers, contracts — professional Urdu for offices.
topics.note: A note on گاہک. گاہک (gaahak — customer) rules business — گاہک ہی بادشاہ (the customer is king). Master it syllable by syllable; clients notice the effort and reward it.
paras: Workplaces run on roles: نوکری (job), دفتر (office), باس (boss), گاہک (customer), ساتھی (colleague). میری نوکری (my job is) introduces your profession; دفتر کہاں ہے؟ finds any office. Roles first, tasks second.

Meetings move business: میٹنگ (meeting), معاہدہ (contract/deal), دستخط (signature). میٹنگ کل صبح (meeting tomorrow morning) — confirm with ٹھیک ہے، آؤں گا (okay, I'll come). Meetings open with السلام علیکم and close with شکریہ.

Money talks plainly: منافع (profit), نقصان (loss), تنخواہ (salary), چھٹی (leave). تنخواہ کب ملتی ہے؟ (when is payday?) — asked smiling, everywhere. Business Urdu respects directness wrapped in politeness.
Digital tools connect all: ای میل (email), فون (phone), پیغام (message). ای میل دیکھیے (please check email) — then کامیابی (success) follows effort. Professional Urdu: formal words, warm heart.
topics.title: Urdu for work and business

topics.desc: Ghalib, mushairas, Eid — reclaim the Urdu your family carried. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Start with sounds you half-know: family words, food names, festival greetings. Heritage ears remember more than they admit — recognition unlocks fast, then production follows.
faqs.q: I understand but can't speak — help?

faqs.a: غالب (Ghalib) — the Diwan-e-Ghalib, Urdu's crown jewel. Learn one sher by heart; Urdu lovers of every age will beam.
faqs.q: What is the one classic to know?

faqs.a: عید مبارک (Eid greetings) and شب برات مبارک (Shab-e-Barat greetings) — festivals are heritage made annual. Greet first, belong instantly.

topics.lede: Ghalib, mushairas, Eid — reclaim the Urdu your family carried.
topics.note: A note on مادری زبان. مادری زبان (maadari zabaan — mother tongue) is Urdu's most emotional phrase — language as mother. میری مادری زبان اردو ہے (my mother tongue is Urdu) is identity declared. Heritage learners don't study Urdu; they come home to it.
paras: Heritage starts with recognition: ورثہ (heritage), بزرگ (elders/ancestors), مادری زبان (mother tongue), تہذیب (culture). Words you heard at knees and kitchens — say them now deliberately. Passive memory converts to active speech within weeks of trying.

Mushairas anchor memory: مشاعرہ (poetry gathering), غالب (Ghalib), اقبال (Iqbal). Every heritage family carries mushaira-Urdu — sher-lines, wah-wahs, tehzeeb. Attend a مشاعرہ with learning ears; childhood vocabulary resurfaces like monsoon wells.

Festivals calendar the year: عید الفطر (Eid al-Fitr), عید الاضحی (Eid al-Adha), شب برات (Shab-e-Barat). Festival kitchens teach fastest — grind, stir, taste, name everything. Heritage you can eat stays learned.

Classics crown the journey: میر (Mir's ghazals), فیض (Faiz's nazms), لکھنؤ to دہلی — the whole adab. One sher memorised outweighs ten lessons completed; heritage learners carry literature, not just language.
topics.title: Urdu for heritage learners

topics.desc: Weeks to chat, months to flow, a year to shine — honest timelines, faster methods. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Survival in 2–4 weeks (greetings, numbers, food), conversation in 3–6 months, comfort in a year — at 20 minutes daily. Consistency beats intensity every time.
faqs.q: How long to hold a conversation?

faqs.a: ع غ ق خ, reading flow, two-gender verbs — جاتا، جاتی. Each surrenders to weeks of drilling — this track attacks every one directly.
Daily contact plus weekly speaking: روز مشق (practise daily), ہفتے بولیے (speak weekly). Apps maintain; conversations advance.

topics.lede: Weeks to chat, months to flow, a year to shine — honest timelines.
topics.note: A note on روز. روز (roz — daily, every day) is the whole secret — روز تھوڑا (a little every day) beats weekend marathons completely. Streaks compound; Urdu rewards the faithful, not the frantic.
paras: Levels ladder clearly: ابتدائی درجہ (beginner — weeks 1–8: survival phrases, core sounds), درمیانی (intermediate — months 3–8: conversations, tenses, reading), اعلیٰ (advanced — month 9+: films, debates, literature). Each درجہ (level) feels impossible until suddenly it doesn't.

Habits beat hours: روز (daily) contact, عادت (habit) over heroics. Fifteen minutes of روز practice — five words, one dialogue, one song line — compounds to fluency while motivation merely visits. Streaks are sacred; protect yours.

Goals steer progress: ہدف (goal) — آغاز (start) with survival, ترقی (progress) monthly measured. This month: order food. Next: small talk. Then: phone calls. Concrete ہدف, celebrated loudly — روانی (fluency) is a trail of kept promises.

Mastery crowns patience: مہارت (mastery), پختہ ارادہ (determination), خود اعتمادی (confidence). A year of faithful days buys comfortable conversation; two buys belonging. Urdu has waited three centuries — it will wait for you, and reward you richly.
topics.title: How long does Urdu take?

topics.desc: Indo-Aryan roots, Persian soul, Hindi twin — Urdu's place in the language family. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Twins, nearly — Urdu and Hindi share grammar and daily words almost fully. Script differs, formal vocabulary differs, hearts are one.
ہندی for daily near-identity, پنجابی next door, then فارسی above all. The urdu-vs-hindi page maps the closest pair.
faqs.q: Which language is closest to Urdu?

faqs.a: Centuries of poetry, courts and culture — فارسی words fill formal Urdu while grammar stays Indo-Aryan. Persian lends soul; Urdu keeps its heart.
faqs.q: Why so much Persian in Urdu?

topics.lede: Indo-Aryan roots, Persian soul, Hindi twin — Urdu's family place.
topics.note: A note on اردو کی شیرینی. اردو کی شیرینی (the sweetness of Urdu) is proverbial — tehzeeb, nazaakat, poetry in daily speech. From mushaira to mohalla, Urdu pride travels worldwide; learners inherit the celebration.
paras: Urdu anchors the north: ہندی (Hindi), پنجابی (Punjabi), بنگالی (Bengali) — cousins, not strangers. Shared roots, shared daily words, proud separate literatures. Learn Urdu and Hindi speech starts echoing.
Persian crowns the register: فارسی lent Urdu thousands of formal words — ادب vocabulary crowns poetry and prose. Daily speech mixes happily. Both registers are real Urdu; learners need both.
Arabic threads the sacred: عربی lent religious and scholarly words — علم، کتاب، دنیا. Three fountains feed one river; drink from all.
Unity crowns diversity: اتحاد (unity) — hundreds of mother tongues, one conversation. Urdu speakers learn English for globe, Urdu for soul. Every language you meet makes your Urdu richer.
topics.title: Urdu among world languages

topics.desc: Twin languages, two scripts — shared speech, split letters, mutual love. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Almost fully for daily speech — گھر، پانی، نام، نہیں are near-identical. Formal registers diverge; street speech is one.
Urdu writes right-to-left in Perso-Arabic; Hindi writes left-to-right in Devanagari. Same tongue, different dress.
Urdu first for tehzeeb, Hindi script second for access. Each halves the other's difficulty — learn one, get the second at a discount.

topics.lede: Twin languages, two scripts — shared speech, split letters.
topics.note: A note on گھر = घर. Urdu گھر (house) and Hindi घर are the SAME word in two scripts — thousands work this way. Learn Urdu's core well and Hindi speech needs no learning at all.
paras: The twins grew as one: اردو bloomed in courts and camps, हिंदी spread across the north. Same grammar, same daily words — Urdu drank Persian while Hindi drank Sanskrit. History in every sentence.
Shared words delight learners: گھر/घर (house), پانی/पानी (water), نام/नाम (name), دوست/दोस्त (friend) — identical in speech. Core vocabulary IS shared; learn one list, own two languages.

Split scripts mark the border: Urdu's right-to-left curves against Hindi's left-to-right headline. مجھے (mujhe — to-me) against मुझे, ہاں (haan) against हाँ — same sounds, different clothes. Drill both scripts; cross freely.

Greetings show both faces: السلام علیکم stands Urdu-warm while नमस्ते stands Hindi-classic — yet each understands the other's instantly. Twins recognise twins; learn either with love and both reward you.
topics.title: Urdu vs Hindi

topics.desc: Dialogues, songs and drama serials — learn Urdu the Lollywood way. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Dramas and realistic films — clear speech, everyday words, repeatable ڈائیلاگ (dialogues). Pakistani drama teaches natural speech like no textbook.
Watch once with subtitles for story, again pausing to shadow dialogues, songs on loop for sounds. Three passes per episode: story, speech, song.
faqs.q: How do I learn from dramas?

faqs.a: Start with famous lines — short, dramatic, unforgettable. Drama dialogues stick like songs; mimicry is fluency's shortcut.

topics.lede: Dialogues, songs and drama serials — Urdu the Lollywood way.
topics.note: A note on لولی وڈ. لولی وڈ (Lollywood — Lahore's film world) plus Karachi's drama serials rule Urdu screens — stories that cross borders, dialogues quoted for decades. Watch and belong.
paras: Screens are Urdu's second classroom: فلم (film), ڈرامہ (drama serial), سینما (cinema hall) — drama nights are festivals. اداکار (actors) and اداکارہ (actresses) are family members; ہدایت کار (directors) are debated like philosophers. Watch and belong.

Genres teach registers: محبت (romance) speaks softly, مزاح (comedy) snaps jokes, ایکشن (action) barks orders. Romance first — gentle pace, tender words; comedy second — speed and slang; action last — glory without subtlety.

Dialogues drill memory: ڈائیلاگ (dialogue) — repeat famous lines until they own you. Drama dialogues are realism with punch; delivering one correctly earns applause everywhere. Shadow the stars shamelessly.

Music melts resistance: موسیقی (music), گیت (songs), قوالی (qawwali) — learn lyrics line by line, sing them wrong then right. مداح (fans) sing together; join them. Screen Urdu is joyful Urdu — and joyful Urdu sticks forever.
topics.title: Learning from Pakistani cinema

topics.desc: Friends, lovers, weddings — the Urdu of hearts, spoken truly. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: دوست (male friend), سہیلی (female friend) — then پیار (love) and محبت (romance) as bonds deepen. Friendship words first; romance follows naturally.
شادی (wedding), نکاح (marriage ceremony) — دولہا (groom), دلہن (bride). شادی مبارک (wedding greetings) blesses every couple.
faqs.q: How do I talk about weddings?

faqs.a: معافی (forgiveness) — مجھے معاف کیجیے (please forgive me), then صلح (peace). Reconciliations run deep and warm; ask sincerely, receive fully.

topics.lede: Friends, lovers, weddings — the Urdu of hearts, spoken truly.
topics.note: A note on پیار vs محبت. پیار (pyaar) is broad love — family, friends, humanity; محبت (muhabbat) leans romantic. تمہارے پیار کا شکریہ (thanks for your love) suits everyone; محبت belongs to one. Urdu loves precisely.
paras: Friendship opens hearts: دوست (male friend), سہیلی (female friend) — میرا دوست (my friend) introduces proudly. Friendships run lifelong and deep; دوستی (friendship) is celebrated in poetry, films and daily chai. Make one friend and gain a hundred phrases.

Romance speaks softly: عاشق (boyfriend/lover), معشوقہ (girlfriend/beloved), پیار (love). Urdu romance favours poetry over bluntness — ghazals teach the register better than textbooks. Learn gently; speak truly.

Weddings unite families: شادی (wedding), نکاح (marriage ceremony), دولہا (groom), دلہن (bride). Weddings run for days — music, food, rituals, blessings. شادی مبارک (wedding congratulations) is your ticket to the feast.

Bonds deepen and mend: پیار (love), محبت (romance), زندگی (life) — میری زندگی (my life) means my beloved. And when bonds strain: معافی (forgiveness), صلح (peace). Hearts forgive spaciously; ask with folded hands.
topics.title: Talking about relationships

topics.desc: Spaced repetition, topic decks, daily streaks — flashcards that actually work. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: پھر پھر (again and again) — but spaced: 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 30 days. وقفہ (spacing) beats cramming; یادداشت (memory) loves intervals.
Five to ten per topic — quality over quantity. Master one کارڈ deck fully before opening the next; half-known decks rot.
روز (daily) short sessions — ten minutes, every day, no exceptions. Streaks compound; بھولنا (forgetting) loses to routine.

topics.lede: Spaced repetition, topic decks, daily streaks — flashcards that work.
topics.note: A note on دہرائی. دہرائی (dohraai — revision, repeating) is Urdu's own word for spaced review — recalling again, and again, at widening intervals. The language itself teaches the method: revisit, widen, remember.
paras: Cards carry memory: کارڈ (card) — one word, one side; meaning, the other. یادداشت (memory) strengthens with every recall; بھولنا (forgetting) is just unreviewed memory. Build decks per topic — greetings, food, verbs — and review each separately.
Spacing schedules success: وقفہ (interval) — review new cards tomorrow, then in three days, seven, thirty. پھر پھر (again and again), but wider each time. Cramming fills hours; spacing fills years.
Rhythms sustain streaks: روز (daily) quick decks, ہفتہ وار (weekly) full reviews, ماہانہ (monthly) championships. Ten daily minutes beat Sunday marathons; streaks turn study into عادت (habit).

Scores gamify growth: نمبر (marks), مقابلہ (contest), کامیابی (achievement) — even ہار (defeat) teaches. Quiz yourself, beat yesterday's score, celebrate loudly. Flashcards are games that pay in fluency.
